newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl coalition agrees three-point tax plan.
newsitem.headline: Kohl coalition agrees three-point tax plan.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition government agreed on Friday to a basic three-point tax strategy to shore up state finances next year and implement a major tax reform in 1999.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) and junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) issued a joint statement setting out their plans. The main points are as follows:
-- The coalition has decided to stress further savings measures to make up a budget gap caused by the recalcitrance of the opposition SDP (Social Democrats).
-- The reduction of the solidarity surcharge will not be possible until January 1, 1998, for the same reasons.
-- The coalition will institute its comprehensive tax reform in January 1999, as foreseen in the government's programme for more jobs and growth.

FDP leaders said earlier that a planned reduction in the solidarity surcharge next year would have to be postponed after the coalition decided against a hike in petroleum taxes to cover a 10 billion mark revenue shortfall.

The financing gap arose after Finance Minister Theo Waigel and the SPD failed to agree on the 1997 tax bill, the one part of the jobs and growth programme which the SPD could have blocked through its majority in the upper house of parliament.
As a result wealth taxes -- ruled unconstitutional by a court -- will lapse next year, and an increase in child benefits will go ahead automatically.
The deal appears also to settle a row between the CDU/CSU and the FDP over the timing of the tax reform, which the FDP had wanted to go ahead in 1998 -- an election year.
Coalition leaders were holding a news conference to explain their tax decisions.
